lesson.title: 0.775 Volts: The Odd Reference Behind dBu
lesson.summary: dBu measures a voltage relative to a fixed reference of 0.775 V RMS, giving audio engineers a way to compare signal levels across a whole system without constantly restating raw voltages.
lesson.body:
You already know that a decibel is a ratio, and that turning a ratio into a fixed number requires picking a reference to compare against. dBu does exactly that for voltage, using a reference of 0.775 V RMS. That number looks arbitrary until you see where it comes from: it is the voltage that delivers exactly 1 milliwatt of power into a 600 ohm load, an impedance that used to be standard on telephone and professional audio lines. Using P = V^2/R, solve for V: V = sqrt(P times R) = sqrt(0.001 times 600) = sqrt(0.6) = 0.7746 V, which rounds to 0.775 V. Even though very little modern gear actually uses 600 ohm loads anymore, the reference voltage itself stuck around, and decades of meters, mixing consoles, and spec sheets are still calibrated to it.

The formula follows the same pattern as every other decibel measurement you have used: dBu = 20 times log10(V divided by 0.775 V). Because it is defined purely in terms of voltage, dBu works as a level scale on its own, independent of what impedance is actually present in a given piece of gear, unlike power based measurements that only line up with a specific load.

It is worth contrasting dBu with dBV, which you have already covered. dBV references 1 V instead of 0.775 V. Because both scales reference a fixed voltage, the difference between them is a constant, not something that changes with level. For any voltage V, dBu minus dBV equals 20 times log10(1 divided by 0.775), which works out to about 2.2 dB. So 0 dBV, meaning exactly 1 V RMS, equals about +2.2 dBu. That fixed offset is a handy shortcut once you get used to it.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a signal measures 2 V RMS, and you want its level in dBu. Divide first: 2 divided by 0.775 equals 2.581. Take the base ten log: log10(2.581) is about 0.4117. Multiply by 20: 0.4117 times 20 equals 8.23. So a 2 V RMS signal sits at about +8.23 dBu.

One number worth memorizing as an anchor point: professional line level, commonly specified as +4 dBu, corresponds to 0.775 times 10 raised to the power of (4 divided by 20), which is 0.775 times 1.5849, or about 1.228 V RMS. Consumer gear typically runs quieter and is usually specified in dBV instead. Having a fixed, agreed upon reference like this is what lets a spec sheet, a console meter, and a cable running between two pieces of gear all describe the same signal level in the same language, which becomes essential once you start chasing noise and distortion numbers through a signal chain in the chapters ahead.
